taxonomyNote: NatureServe uses Snapping Turtle and notes the 'common' adjective was dropped (Crother et al. 2008); some authors have proposed splitting the Florida population (C. osceola).
fieldMarks: Upper shell saw-toothed at the rear, usually under 36 cm (max nearly 50 cm)
Tail as long as or longer than the shell, with a crest of large bony scales
Large head with hooked jaws; small lower shell (plastron) leaves limbs exposed
Hatchlings rough-shelled with conspicuous ridges, looking like a dead leaf
behavior: Mostly on the bottom; younger animals and far-northern turtles sometimes bask
Decreases activity in late summer, relatively inactive in winter, resumes about April
Females may travel up to several km to nest, often in open soft soil far from water
Eats many vertebrates, invertebrates and plants
habitat: All freshwater habitats, especially soft mud bottoms with abundant vegetation or submerged brush and logs; also brackish water.
range: East of the Rockies from the Canadian border to the Gulf and Atlantic; in Canada mainland Nova Scotia, southern New Brunswick, southern and central Québec and Ontario, southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan. Introduced in the western US and Canada.
